bio.en: Pete Kazanjy is the author of Founding Sales - the book Lenny recommends to every B2B founder - and runs the Modern Sales Pros community; he is also CEO and founder of Atrium, a sales-analytics SaaS.
bio.zh: Pete Kazanjy 是《创始销售》（Founding Sales）一书的作者——这本书是 Lenny 推荐给每一位 B2B 创始人的必读——他运营着 Modern Sales Pros 销售社区，同时也是销售分析 SaaS 公司 Atrium 的创始人兼 CEO。

summary.en: Pete dismantles the myth that sales is only for natural-born sellers, reframing it as a learnable craft centered on founder-led selling. He explains why founders should sell early - to shape the product, learn positioning, and build a repeatable motion before hiring - and offers a concrete heuristic: hire your first salesperson once you reliably close 15-25% of contacts. The episode is a tactical guide to modern, founder-driven B2B sales.
summary.zh: Pete 打破了“销售只属于天生销售员”的迷思，将销售重新定义为一种可习得的手艺，核心在于创始人亲自销售。他解释了创始人为何应当尽早销售——以便打磨产品、学习定位，并在招人之前建立可复制的动作——并给出了具体启发式：当你能稳定成交 15-25% 的接触对象时，就该招聘第一位销售。本期是关于现代创始人驱动型 B2B 销售的实战指南。

turns.en: The way that I think about the book, Founding Sales, I like to think of it as the sequel to Eric Eric Ries's The Lean Startup or Steve Blank's Four Steps to the Epiphany or Startup Owner's Manual or whatever, where if you think about the stages, and this is all B2B, if you think about the stages that a product goes through, it's one, you've got to know what problem you're solving and validate that, and it's got to be real. It can't be like, "Oh, well, I thought I had this problem," it's got to be validated. That's customer development, that's customer research, and that's more of a product management function. And then there's building the minimum feature set in order to prove that maybe technology can fit to this problem and solve it. (00:10:26): That's how we create value as technologists, is piecing together technology and code or bits and atoms and what have you in order to solve a problem that people have. But then the next step is like, "Cool. Now, I've got to get someone to pay for this and I've got to do that in a reliable fashion and I've got to do it in a scalable fashion," and so there's a little bit of a loop there. It's a loop, where the minimum viable version of your product is probably going to suck and then in order to get to the minimum valuable step, you've got to be interfacing with a lot of customers and that's a sales behavior, getting in front of people and being like, "Hey, I think you probably have this problem if you look like these other folks right here." (00:11:11): The point is is that you can't outsource that behavior, the founder's got to do that stuff. A lot of people ask me that question, "Well, I suck at sales," or, "I'm afraid to talk to people," or, "Interfacing with non-friendly parties makes me uncomfortable." The way to think about it is, I forget who the person was who said, "Startups versus incumbents is a race between can innovation get to distribution before distribution can get to innovation?" So, this is a related concept where as a founder, it's going to be way easier for you to get good, or minimally viable good, at selling by having interactions with non-friendly parties and having commercial conversations and asking for money in exchange for the value delivery. (00:11:58): It's going to be easier for you to do that than it is for some third party to become as expert at the subject matter that you're tackling that you are. (00:12:46): This is why Steve Blank always talks about startups can't get to scale without firing their first VP of sales, it's oftentimes because they skip that step, and so the founder's like, "Hey, man, I'm going to pour a little bit of sales on this, hire some sales leader or whatever, some sort of seller, and outsource this." You're playing a game of telephone with that with a third party seller versus even you just want to keep that in one brain to start, then package it, and then when you have a repeatable while loop, a selling while loop, then package it and hand it to someone else. So, that's my diatribe on why founders have to do this.
turns.zh:
关于《创始人销售》这本书，我认为它可以被视为埃里克·里斯（Eric Ries）的《精益创业》、史蒂夫·布兰克（Steve Blank）的《四步创业法》或《创业者手册》等作品的延续。如果你从B2B领域的视角来思考产品的发展阶段，就会发现产品需要经历以下几个阶段：首先，你必须明确要解决的问题并验证其真实性。这绝不是空想出来的问题，而是必须经过验证的——这属于客户开发和市场调研的范畴，更多地属于产品管理的职责。接下来，你需要构建最小可行产品（MVP）来验证技术是否能解决实际问题。这正是我们作为技术人员创造价值的方式——通过拼凑技术和代码、原子与粒子，来解决用户痛点。然而，真正的挑战在于如何让用户为此买单，并且要以可靠且可扩展的方式实现这一目标。这并非“产品完成后就能交付，坐享其成”的过程，而是一个闭环。MVP可能一开始很糟糕，但为了达成最小可行价值（MVV），你必须与大量客户互动——这本身就是销售行为，意味着要主动走出去，向潜在客户说明“如果你们和这些用户群体相似，可能面临同样的问题”。

关键在于，创始人不能将这些销售行为外包出去。许多人问我：“我不擅长销售”、“害怕与人交谈”或“面对不友好的客户感到不适”。我的建议是，忘掉是谁说过“初创公司与传统企业的竞争，关键在于创新能否在分销前完成？”这个类比。这里有个相关概念：作为创始人，通过与不友好的客户互动、进行商业谈判并要求以价值交换资金，比让第三方专家更容易掌握销售技能。因为创始人早期（以Atrium为例）需要开发数据驱动的销售管理软件，帮助销售经理和团队利用指标和数据提升团队绩效。我认为这类似于Datadog和Amplitude，但专注于销售团队。我可能是全球销售分析领域的专家。2016年和2017年我们开发这款产品时，先不说我已经掌握了最小可行销售方法，如果让别人成为专家再去市场推广，结果肯定不理想。

这就是为什么史蒂夫·布兰克总说初创公司不解雇首位销售副总裁就无法实现规模化。通常是因为他们跳过了这个关键步骤。创始人会想：“我要投入一点销售资源，聘请销售领导或销售人员，把这事外包出去。”但这根本行不通，至少在前几十个客户阶段不可行。这会失去反馈循环，失去学习机会。
你的信息不符合市场需求，诸如此类的问题。你这是在和第三方卖家玩“传话游戏”，而你本该先把这些想法整合在自己脑中，然后进行打包。等你形成一个可重复的销售闭环后，再将成果交付给其他人。所以，这就是我对创业者为何必须亲力亲为的吐槽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to try to summarize the reasons that you should be doing this and it sounds like there's so many. One is figure out what you should actually be building, that's a reason founders should be selling, two is learn how to position and pitch and sell, three is figure out what you could teach your salesperson when you hire them. Is that a summary of why you should be selling as a founder for a while?
turns.zh: 我本来想总结一下你应该这么做的原因，听起来原因太多了。第一，弄清楚你真正应该开发的产品，这就是创始人应该销售产品的原因；第二，学习如何定位、推销和销售产品；第三，确定你招募销售人员后能教给他们什么。这是否总结了创始人暂时转向销售岗位的原因？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. One, it's going to help you with your product development because you're not going to have that abstracted, for sure, two, you're going to be the person who's going to figure out how to talk about it in an effective way, and then three, it's going to make it such that you can package that up such that other human... Because that's the way that B2B startups scale, is it's not WhatsApp or Twitter or Airbnb or whatever, where you have this scalability via marketing, the way that B2B organizations scale primarily is by adding more salespeople who then have customer-facing meetings with prospects. (00:14:32): And then you cap out with the number of hours that are in the week, there's only four or 50 hours in the week, especially as a seller because you interface with other people during business hours, and so the way that you scale up is by just adding more salespeople. So, that's why packaging that up is really important, because then you're going to shove it into the brains of two more salespeople, and then once they're successful, you're going to go to four, and then once they're successful, you're going to go to eight, and then once they're successful, you're going to go to 16.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。首先，这能帮助你进行产品开发，因为你不必再进行抽象思考。其次，你将成为那个能有效传达产品价值的人。而第三，这能让你把产品打包成易于理解的方案，方便其他人……因为B2B初创公司的扩张方式不同于WhatsApp、Twitter、Airbnb等公司。B2B公司主要通过增加销售人员来实现增长，而这些销售人员需要与潜在客户进行面对面的沟通。（00:14:32）由于一周的时间有限（通常只有四十小时），尤其是销售人员需要在工作时间与客户沟通，因此扩展规模的关键在于增加销售人员数量。因此，打包产品至关重要，这样你就能将方案传授给两名销售人员。一旦他们取得成功，再增加到四名，如此循环递增。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talk about this while loop concept, which I love. What are signs that it's time to hire your first salesperson? It begs the question, when do I do this?
turns.zh: 你提到的这个“循环往复”的概念，我很喜欢。那么，什么时候该招聘首位销售人员呢？这就引出了一个问题：何时该采取行动？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I'm not a software engineer, but I like to use technical metaphors with technical audiences because I think it's helpful, so it's like when it runs on your local, now it's time to see if it reproduces over here, so if it reliably runs on your local and it doesn't air out, so then what would the definition of not erroring out look like? So, generally speaking, it is to contingent on your sales motion, but it's going to be that you can reliably, at a pretty okay win rate, so maybe 15% or 20% or 25%, turn first meetings into eventual customers and do that in a reliable fashion. It's not like, "I engaged 10 arms-length parties and I got two customers closed." It's like, "Hey, that's great. That's a good start. 5X that, 10X that." (00:16:08): Take 50 at-bats, take 100 at-bats, and now that you know that you reliably, for every cohort of ten first meetings, what's known in sales land as opportunities, for every cohort of 10 that you engage, are you closing 1, are you closing 1.5, are you closing 2, or are you closing 2.5, if you're in there? But if you're at like, "For every 30 I interact with, I close one," well, it seems like that's probably pretty inefficient, unless you're selling $500,000 deals or something like that. So, it's at the point where it feels like it's statistically significant, it feels like it's repeatable, because what you're going to then do is now it feels like it's a safe bet to try to abstract that out to somebody else. (00:16:54): Because the only way we're going to get to success is we're not going to have Lenny go and sell from morning, noon to night. What we're going to do is we're going to take the information out of Lenny's brain and we're going to put it into slides and we're going to put it into scripts and we're going to put it into email templates and all that sort of stuff, and then we're going to shove that into the brain of two more reps and see if now we can get it to run in the cloud, in the sales cloud here. And then to start out, it may fail, the same way you're like, "Cool, it runs on my local. Uh-oh, it breaks over here. Why?" And then that's the next stage is now you're figuring out how to get those other folks to sell as successfully as you have, and that becomes the next job. (00:17:39): Actually, this is the presentation I gave at Brianne's SaaS School, if you Google it's just called Founder-led Selling, it's available online. Essentially, there's a bunch of stages in the B2B maturity journey and you have to go through them in order to get to the next one, if you jump stages, you're hosed. So, in this case, if you know that you can reliably sell this yourself, that's great. Then, the next thing to do is get at least a couple people reliably selling, as well as you, not 10, because you're never going to get 2 successful if you're trying to onboard 10 concurrently. And then if you get those 2 successful, now you've earned the right to go to 4, 8, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我不是软件工程师，但我喜欢在技术听众面前用技术比喻，因为我觉得这很有帮助。比如，当它在本地环境中运行良好后，现在就该看看它能否在异地环境中重现成功。假设在本地环境中运行稳定且无故障，那么“不出现错误”的定义应该是什么呢？一般来说，这取决于你的销售策略，但关键在于能否以相当高的胜率（比如15%、20%或25%）将首次会面转化为最终客户，并且要做到可靠。不是那种“接触了10个潜在客户，成交了两个”的结果，而是要积极反思：“嘿，这不错，是个好的开始。再提高5倍、10倍效果。”（00:16:08）：进行50次尝试，100次尝试后，当你知道每10次首次会面（即销售术语中的“机会”）就能成功成交1个、1.5个、2个或2.5个客户时，说明你已经达到了统计学意义上的显著水平，也具备了可复制性。接下来，你就可以放心地将这些成功经验抽象化并分享给其他人了。（00:16:54）：因为我们要想取得成功，不能指望莱尼从早到晚不停地销售。我们要做的是，将莱尼脑中的信息提取出来，整理成幻灯片、销售脚本、邮件模板等，然后再传授给另外两名销售代表，看看能否在“销售云”中成功复现。起初可能会失败，就像你会说：“不错，本地环境运行正常。哎呀，异地环境出问题了。为什么呢？” 接下来就是如何让其他人也能像你一样成功销售，这才是下一步的工作。（00:17:39）：实际上，这是我在布莱恩的SaaS学校做的演讲，谷歌搜索“Founder-led Selling”就能找到，线上有完整内容。B2B成熟度之旅本质上分为多个阶段，你必须按顺序完成每个阶段。跳过阶段只会导致失败。就拿你现在的情况来说，如果你能成功独立销售，那很棒。接下来要做的就是让至少两名销售人员能像你一样稳定销售，当然不是10个一起，因为同时上手10个的话，成功率很难达到2个。等这两人成功后，你才有资格扩展到4、8个等规模的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this heuristic that you shared that you want to get to about 15 to 25% of contacts closing to a customer. I see you shaking your thumb. I think that's really useful. So, it's a bit less than a third and doing 50 to 100 attempts is roughly where you want to be?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你提到的这个启发式方法，即让15%到25%的潜在客户成功转化为客户。我看到你正在摇动大拇指。我觉得这真的很有用。那就是转化率略低于三分之一，进行50到100次尝试，大概就是这个目标吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Yeah. Importantly, what you don't want to do is, and I think probably a lot of the product managers who like to listen to Lenny's Podcast here might appreciate this, is you want to bring on cohorts of users and then see what's going on, then learn, and then bring on new co cohorts of users. So, going and doing 100 at-bats and then being like, "Did it work or did it not?" Versus, "Hey, let's have 10 for prospect and try to get 10 first meetings," have all those interactions, see how your conversations land, see how the discovery questions are evoking the right response or not the right response, see how your slides land, see how your demo lands, all that sort of stuff. (00:19:15): If it's working well and you're getting to the next stage, "This is great, I would love to introduce you to my boss," that's a good sign. If it's like, "I'm just not getting it." Cool, back to the drawing board, versus doing 100 all at once and being like, "Now, did it work?" We want to break it up and then constantly just be iterating, iterating, iterating. Again, I think your audience might appreciate this, the way to think of a sales motion, so sales motion is a fancy-pants way of describing just all the things that you do in order to take a prospect and bring them through the sales process and then eventually close them. One helpful way to think about it is kind of like software and what you want to be doing is constantly updating it. Oh, that was a really interesting question that the prospect asked right there, I didn't have a good answer for it and moreover, I didn't have a slide for it. (00:20:04): You know what I should do? I should make a slide that handles that objection so I can show it to them visually and also, it'll help give me guardrails and a talk track and that'll be nice. So, I'm going to do that and then I'm going to update the source code. Now, my sales motion has been updated. And then the next loop through, ideally the next time that person says, "Oh, I don't know, Lenny, it doesn't really sound like X, Y, Z," you're like, "Oh, a lot of people say that, but here, if you look over here, you can see this." "Oh yeah, that's a really good point." "Wonderful. So, as the next step, let's go ahead and talk to your boss." So, now your sales motion has been updated and the collateral's been updated and now, we're being more effective sellers. You're just going to do that dozens and dozens and dozens and dozens and dozens of time before you have a repeatable sales motion.
turns.zh: 是的。重要的是，你不想做的是——我觉得很多喜欢听Lenny播客的听众可能会赞同这一点——你不想一次性接触一大批用户，然后观察结果、总结经验，再去接触新一批用户。就像打100次棒球，然后问“这次成功了吗？”相比之下，先接触10个潜在客户，尝试安排首次会面，再进行所有互动——观察谈话效果如何，探索性问题是否能引发正确回应，演示文稿和产品演示是否到位等等——要好得多。如果进展顺利，客户会说：“我想把你介绍给我老板。”这就是一个积极信号。如果对方说：“我还是不明白。”那就回去重新调整，而不是一次性尝试100次然后问：“这次成功了吗？”我们需要分步骤推进，不断迭代。再说，我觉得听众可能会欣赏这种思考销售流程的方式。销售流程本质上就是你为推动潜在客户完成销售流程并最终达成交易所做的一切准备工作。一个有效的思考方式是把它比作软件开发——你需要不断更新迭代。比如，潜在客户提出了一个很有趣的问题，而你当时没有好的答案，甚至没有相关的演示文稿。（00:20:04）你知道该怎么做吗？你应该制作一个能应对这种异议的演示文稿，这样既能直观展示，又能为你提供框架和谈话思路。这就很好了。接下来，你要更新源代码。现在，销售流程已经更新，相关资料也调整好了，我们就能更高效地推进销售了。在下一次互动中，如果对方说：“哦，Lenny，我不太明白，X、Y、Z听起来不像啊。”你就可以说：“哦，很多人都这么说，但如果你看这边，你会发现……” “哦，对啊，这真是个好观点。” “太棒了。那么，下一步，让我们去和你的老板谈谈吧。”这样一来，你的销售流程就更新了，相关资料也完善了，我们的销售效率也会显著提升。在形成可复制的销售流程之前，你还需要反复进行这样的迭代过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting is with this heuristic, two-thirds of the time, it's not going to work out.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，用这种启发式方法，三分之二的情况下都不会成功。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Nope.
turns.zh: 不会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, a lot of times, they're going to be like, "Ah, I don't get this, leave me alone." Is there other leading indicators that tell you that you're improving, knowing that only a third or maybe a fifth of the time it'll work out? Is it talking to the boss off more often, what else do you look for?
turns.zh: 所以，很多时候，他们会说：“啊，我不明白，别烦我了。”有没有其他领先指标能告诉你正在进步呢？要知道，只有三分之一甚至五分之一的情况下才会成功。是更频繁地与老板沟通吗？你还关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Totally. So, what are the leading indicators of success? Because if you're only looking at lagging indicators, again, it's probably a it's a funnel on a new feature, so the opportunity is an at-bat or a potential transaction, and so usually what you do is you model out the stages in your opportunity. So, generally, there will be different stages depending on the sales motion. So, use Atrium as an example, we sell on customer data. It takes five minutes to turn on an Atrium account, it's really helpful for folks. They just sign in, they OAuth with Salesforce, great. So, a really important stage in our sales motion is, we call it data light, has data been lit up? So, that's a stage, we have a discovery stage, we have a data light stage, we have what we call a preview stage, are we previewing it with the staff? Then, we get to a commercial discussion. (00:22:08): So, you can measure how you're getting to those stages, which is somebody lands on whatever page that Lenny was in charge of at Airbnb and did they click on the right thing and do they get to the next thing and did they get to the next thing, get to the next thing? So, in sales, it's kind of the same thing. So, the more sophisticated version of this is looking at stage conversions, what have you, the less sophisticated version of it, which early on, I think is an appropriate way of doing it, is like, "Hey, man, are we getting second dates?" So, just metaphorize it to Hinge or Coffee Meets Bagel or whatever the more recent one is, it's like, "Are we getting the second dates? Are we getting the third dates? Because if we're not getting the second dates, probably something's amiss there." (00:22:51): So, what we want to do is we want to say, "Great, of all of our ten first meetings, how many gets to second meetings?" It would be great, the lagging indicator is 2 wins out of 10 or what have you, but I'm going to come into these conversations and out of my ten first meetings, I want seven of them to get to the second meeting. And then of those seven, maybe I want 4.5 of them to get to the third meeting, and then ultimately, I want 2 or 3 to win. That's the way to think about that, those are the leading indicators. So, as those conversions get better like, "Man, I'm not getting any second dates. Oh, okay, cool, you need a haircut or you need a shower," and the same applies to your sales motion, as well. Your message is not landing, you're targeting the wrong people, what's going on here? You need to think about it.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。完全正确。那么，成功的领先指标是什么？因为如果你只看滞后指标的话，再说一次，这可能就像新功能的漏斗阶段，所以机会就是一次尝试或潜在交易。因此，通常你会对机会的各个阶段进行建模。一般来说，根据销售流程的不同，会有不同的阶段。以Atrium为例，我们销售的是客户数据。开通Atrium账户只需五分钟，对用户非常有帮助。他们只需登录，使用Salesforce的OAuth授权，就可以了。所以，在我们的销售流程中，有一个非常重要的阶段，我们称之为"数据启用阶段"，即数据是否已经启用？这就是一个阶段。我们还有发现阶段、数据启用阶段，以及我们称之为预览阶段，即我们是否在向员工预览产品？然后，我们进入商业讨论阶段。（00:22:08）：你可以衡量人们如何进入这些阶段，比如有人访问了Lenny在Airbnb负责的页面，他们是否点击了正确的链接，是否进入了下一个页面，是否进入了下下个页面？在销售中，这道理是一样的。更复杂的版本是观察阶段转换情况，比如第二次约会成功率是多少，但更初级的版本——我认为这在早期是合适的做法——就是问：“嘿，伙计，我们能成功约会第二次吗？”（00:22:51）：所以，我们想说，“太好了，我们十次初次会面中有多少能进入第二次会面？”滞后指标可能是10次中有2次成功，但我要说的是，在我的十次初次会面中，我希望有七次能进入第二次会面。在这七次中，或许我希望有4.5次能进入第三次会面，最终我希望有2到3次能成功。这就是思考方式，这些就是领先指标。所以，当这些转化率提高时，比如“天哪，我一次第二次约会都约不成。哦，好吧，不错，你需要理发或者洗澡了”，同样适用于你的销售流程。你的信息传达不到位，目标人群选错了，这是怎么回事？你需要思考一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You need a better pickup line.
turns.zh: 你需要更好的搭讪台词。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: There you go. Now, you're not even getting first dates, man, go all the way up to you need a better Hinge profile picture. You're just not getting any matches, ew.
turns.zh: 就是这样。现在，你连第一次约会都约不成了，伙计，你得从头再来，你需要更好的Hinge个人资料图片。你根本就没法配对，真恶心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a founder, do you have to get good at sales? A lot of founders are like, "Oh my God, we're going to do PLG. We're going to be self-serve, freemium, we don't need sales. I'm just going to let people figure it out." Is it a requirement of a B2B business to get good at sales as a founder?
turns.zh: 作为创始人，你必须擅长销售吗？很多创始人会说：“天哪，我们要做PLG。我们要提供自助服务，免费增值，我们不需要销售。我就让用户自己去搞定。”作为B2B企业的创始人，擅长销售是必须的吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I would say you don't have to get good at it, you just have to get non-zero at it. There's this really great article on Lenny's newsletter on adding a sales organization to a self-serve product that Lenny had me write and then he edited the heck out of it, and it's really a fantastic asset. But what I would say there is that there are a lot of PLG or self-serve motions out there that they've stagnated themselves because they didn't add the sales piece to it. I would encourage people to read that article, I forget what it's called, you added a really cool name.
turns.zh: 我想说，你不必精通销售，只需做到不输于别人就行。莱尼的时事通讯上有一篇很棒的文章，讲如何为自助产品添加销售组织，我写了那篇文章，然后莱尼对它进行了深度润色，这确实是一份极具价值的资源。但我要指出的是，许多PLG或自助产品策略之所以停滞不前，往往是因为没有及时引入销售团队。我鼓励大家去读那篇文章，忘了名字叫什么了，不过你起的标题确实很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, The Transition: Layering on Sales to Product-led Growth.
turns.zh: 哦，《转型：为产品主导型增长叠加销售力量》。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: See, you're good at naming things.
turns.zh: 看吧，你很擅长给东西起名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's inspired by David Sack's The Cadence, which I love for how to operate.
turns.zh: 这源自大卫·萨克的《节奏》一书，我很喜欢书中提到的运营理念。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: There you go. That is a great article. So, it's not that you have to be great, you just have to recognize that it's important. A good example of this would be, probably the most famous example of an organization that maybe didn't get sales religion as quickly as they should have would be Dropbox. Dropbox has phenomenal early sales leadership. One of our investors here at Atrium is a gentleman named Mike Marg, he's a partner at Craft Ventures, he was an early sales manager and leader there, Kyle Parrish was the head of sales at Figma, Marissa Fuhrer is over at Figma, as well. There's all these just absolutely fantastic Dropbox folks, but the problem was is that the organization, from a product standpoint, never put all as many calories behind product development that would support the ability to sell to across an entire organization. (00:25:48): So, the way that I try to succinctly describe that is never mistake your lead gen for your business. I think the good news is that a lot of people took a lot of lumps there and folks have learned that, maybe Slack almost missed that, but then they brought in a bunch of Salesforce folks and other folks, actually, Mike Marg was also an early sales manager at Slack, as well, and really got a religion around that. Because it turns out that people paying 19 bucks a month or 29 bucks a month or what have you is really great, but getting to a $50,000 or a $100,000 or a $250,000 contract, that's where big ARR numbers start racking up, and organizations want to talk to a human in order to navigate that. (00:26:34): So, PLG is great for landing and permeating an organization and there's a bunch of great... Craft invests in this like crazy, so Scratchpad is a great example of very bottoms-up. Atrium's pretty bottoms up, as well. It's like, I don't know, what is the Silicon Valley joke, middle out or whatever, because we land with sales managers and SDR managers. What you're doing is you're solving the problem that the user has, but the problem is the user doesn't necessarily have large budgetary authority, so you can get them stoked up, but then you've got to talk to the person who's got the purse strings, and so that's going to require sales. That's okay.
turns.zh: 就是这样。这篇文章确实很棒。所以，关键不在于你必须做到完美，而在于你要认识到它的重要性。一个典型的例子或许是Dropbox，这个组织可能没有及时建立起销售文化。Dropbox早期有出色的销售领导团队。我们Atrium的一位投资者叫迈克·马格，是Craft Ventures的合伙人，他曾是Dropbox的早期销售经理。凯尔·帕里什曾是Figma的销售主管，玛丽莎·富勒也供职于Figma。Dropbox有很多出色的团队成员，但问题在于，从产品角度来看，组织没有投入足够的精力开发支持全公司销售的功能。（00:25:48）所以，我试图简洁地概括为：永远不要把潜在客户开发误当作业务本身。好消息是，很多人在这方面吃了不少苦头，现在大家都意识到这一点。Slack差点就犯了同样的错误，但后来他们引入了Salesforce的团队成员，实际上，迈克·马格也曾是Slack的早期销售经理，并成功树立了这一理念。因为事实证明，每月支付19美元、29美元或其他金额的用户固然不错，但要达成5万美元、10万美元或25万美元的合同，才是ARR数字开始攀升的关键，而客户通常希望与真人沟通以完成交易。（00:26:34）所以，PLG模式很适合渗透和渗透整个组织，有很多优秀的案例……Craft Ventures对此投入巨大，Scratchpad就是一个自下而上的典范。Atrium也是如此。我不知道硅谷那句笑话怎么说的，是自上而下还是其他的，因为我们从销售经理和SDR经理入手。你解决的是用户的问题，但用户往往没有足够的预算权限，所以你可以激发他们的热情，但最终还是要和掌控资金的人沟通，这就需要销售团队了。没关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to punctuate that, basically 100% of B2B companies end up building a sales team?
turns.zh: 补充一点，基本上100%的B2B公司最终都会组建销售团队？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I would say that's the case. It's more of a question of when versus if, so even the really famous ones like Atlassian. Atlassian, they had a sales organization, they just didn't call it a sales organization and they went pretty far without a lot, but instead what they did was they just priced the product breathtakingly low. I think developer tools can oftentimes do this, where because developers are pretty technical, they can adopt product, they don't need handholding in order to adopt a product that is complicated enough to be valuable. Datadog's a good example or New Relic or AppD, but even those guys very early on had meaningful sales organizations. There's a lot of reasons why Datadog ended up winning that market, but their sales organization is no joke. Even developer tools, you might think, cool, well, the developers can just swipe their credit cards. Yeah, they can, but then you're going to be eventually capped there. Look at Snowflake. Snowflake has, I don't know, 500 salespeople, you're going to need a sales org.
turns.zh: 我觉得确实如此。这更多的是一个何时而非是否的问题，就连像Atlassian这样赫赫有名的公司也是如此。Atlassian当时有销售团队，但他们不把它称为销售团队，靠着低价策略走得很远。我认为开发者工具类产品往往能做到这一点，因为开发者技术能力强，他们能自主采用产品，无需过多引导就能接受复杂但有价值的产品。Datadog、New Relic和AppD等公司就是很好的例子，即便这些公司早期也有规模不小的销售团队。Datadog能在市场上胜出的原因有很多，但他们的销售团队绝对不容小觑。再说开发者工具，你可能会想，嗯，开发者直接刷信用卡购买就行了。是的，他们确实可以，但最终会遇到天花板。比如Snowflake，据我所知有500名销售人员，任何产品都需要强大的销售团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's shift a bit to talking about just how to get better at sales, at the scale of sales. I think it's interesting because you don't have a sales background and so you've had to learn how to do this and you did a lot of research and building your business, you've had to get really good at sales. So, maybe a first question, what's the number one tip that you have for getting better at sales?
turns.zh: 接下来我们来谈谈如何提升销售能力，尤其是大规模销售层面的。我觉得这很有意思，因为你没有销售背景，所以必须自学成才。你做了大量研究，打造了自己的业务，必须在销售方面精益求精。首先有个问题，你认为提升销售能力最重要的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: The first chapter of Founding Sales talks about what I call sales mindset changes. Because I think the big thing is it's just so weird, it's just such a weird shift in behavior. Because if you think about it as a product manager or as an engineer or whatever, how many people do you interact with day-to-day? Oh, 6, 10 maybe.
turns.zh: 《Founding Sales》第一章讲的是我所说的销售思维转变。我认为关键在于这是一种非常奇特的行为转变。以产品经理或工程师的视角来看，你每天接触多少人？大概6个、10个人吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not too many.
turns.zh: 接触的人并不多。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: It's always the same people and so it's super comfortable, whereas in sales or anything customer facing, what ends up happening is you're meeting multiple new humans every day, if you're doing it right, and that just is such a mindset shift. You're not going to be able to remember everybody. You're going to have to write it all down. You're going to have to use the CRM for that. You're in the starting blocks on the track. You're in the starting blocks and you have 90 seconds or a couple minutes to form rapport, to make somebody feel like they should trust you and they want to be honest with you. You have to be very focused on activity orientation, whereas engineering and product management, there's does a lot of super deep work. (00:29:52): It's like Paul Graham's Maker versus Manager Schedule. Salespeople have manager schedules, interestingly enough, where what you're doing is you're constantly contact switching, an ideal salesperson's calendar or a founder who's doing sales is 2, 3, 4, maybe 5 customer-facing meetings a day with different humans. And then moreover, then you're having incremental interactions with those folks later on, like later that week or the next week or what have you, so then you have to keep continuity of these multiple parallel conversations. It's a totally different set of skills and so it feels super weird to start out, but what ends up happening is it's just a skill. You just start doing it, you start doing it, you start doing it, and you just become used to it, you become calloused. You're like, "I'm incorrigible now. You put me in an elevator, I can talk to anyone." (00:30:43): So, one, just recognizing it's going to be a pretty big mindset change, and then the second thing you can do is then once you know that there's going to be a mindset change, is you can focus in on making those behaviors be better. So, as an example, one of the things I challenge my staff to do is I call it turbo rapport, it needs a better name. But think about people that you interact with in the world who maybe are a little shields up, they're probably used to interacting with people who are not going to be super nice to them, maybe it's bartenders or a flight attendant or a barista, or fill in the blank. Think about how quickly you can become friends with them, how you can break that down, because that's going to be a really good skill for you to have when you're interacting with a prospect. (00:31:31): And then what that's going to allow you to do is then ask them candid questions about their current situation that either, A, they may know about or, B, you ask provocative questions that make them think about the world in a way maybe that you want them to and realize that they have pain they didn't want or didn't know that they had. My friend, Brett Burson, had this great tweet one at one point where he said, "Think about the things that you do in your day-to-day that are like a pianist, like a piano player, playing scales like, 'Da, da, da, da, da, da.' What is the version of that for selling?" That's rapid rapport building, asking good questions, asking follow-up questions, being willing to ask uncomfortable questions, all those sort of things, and asking for money and then shutting up and waiting for them to answer, all these are very uncomfortable things, but the more you do them, you'll just get good at them.
turns.zh: 老是和同一批人打交道，所以特别自在。但在销售或任何需要面对客户的工作中，你每天都要接触不同的人，若你做得好，确实能转变思维模式。但你不可能记住每个人的名字，必须把所有信息记录下来，靠CRM系统来协助。这就像站在起跑线上，只有90秒或几分钟的时间建立融洽关系，让对方信任你、愿意坦诚相待。你必须高度专注于行动导向，而工程和产品管理则需要深度钻研。（00:29:52）这就像保罗·格雷厄姆提出的"创客与管理者日程表"。销售人员的时间表就是管理者模式，不断切换联系人，理想的销售日程表或创业者兼销售人员的日程表可能是每天与不同客户进行2、3、4次甚至5次面对面会议。随后还要与这些客户进行后续互动，比如当周晚些时候或下周等等。因此，你必须保持多重并行对话的连贯性。这完全是不同的一套技能，刚开始确实很不适应，但最终这只是一项技能。你不断练习，逐渐习惯，变得游刃有余。就像"我现在无药可救了，把我扔进电梯，我也能和任何人聊天"。（00:30:43）首先，要意识到这将是一个巨大的思维转变。第二，一旦意识到这种思维转变，你就可以专注于提升这些行为能力了。比如，我要求员工掌握的"涡轮增压式建立融洽关系"技巧，虽然这个名字不太贴切。但想想那些在生活中可能保持警惕的人——比如酒保、空乘人员、咖啡师等等——你能多快与他们成为朋友，突破他们的防备。这对你与潜在客户互动时将大有裨益。（00:31:31）然后，你就能借此机会坦诚询问他们当前处境，A、他们可能已经了解这些问题，B、提出发人深省的问题，引导他们以你期望的方式看待世界，进而发现他们未曾察觉的痛点。我的朋友布雷特·伯森曾发过一条精彩推文："想想你日常生活中那些像钢琴师般机械重复的动作，比如'达、达、达、达、达、达'。销售中的对应版本是什么呢？"这包括快速建立融洽关系、提出高质量问题、追问后续细节、敢于提出令人不适的问题、索要报价后静待回应等。这些都让人不自在，但多练习就能熟能生巧。

（00:33:31）：你书中最让我改变销售思维的一点，是从试图说服别人购买产品转变为致力于帮助他们，或许这能让他们的生活更轻松。你能谈谈这方面的看法吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I think this is like the, remember the modern sales versus old-school sales thing?
turns.zh: 我觉得这就像是，记得现代销售和传统销售的区别吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: The old-school sales thing is like, "I'm going to sell something to a mark," or the best example of this, "That guy's a great sales guy, he can sell ice to an Eskimo." It's like, "Man, if you're selling ice to an Eskimo, you're an asshole. What is wrong with you? They don't need ice," unless they're visiting Southern California. So, as a seller, the way that I like to frame it to people is that you're a consultant that has a particular predilection for a given solution, your solution. Use Atrium as an example. Atrium's minimum ICP is probably SDRs plus AEs in an organization should probably be at 10 all the way up to 300. So, if someone shows up and they're like, "Man, I've got to get really good at sales, I need to buy your software, Pete," and I'm like, "Cool. How many salespeople do you have?" They're like, "I have one." I'll be like, "Man, I'm not going to sell you Atrium. You're just going to be unhappy, it's going to be dumb, it's going to be a waste of our customer success resources, you're going to churn," all those sort of things. (00:34:56): But if instead what you're doing is you're saying, "Hey, I'm going to go out in the market and I'm going to find the people that have a high proclivity that our technology solves and then I'm going to talk with them about how they're solving that problem right now, and ideally, through a series of questions, I'm going to reveal that to them that they're doing it probably not great. And then once I've revealed to them the fact, through this directed questioning, what's known as discovery, that they have this high magnitude problem, that it is causing them lots of money, that it is a pain in their ass, and then I reveal to them that there is a better way of approaching it and magically enough, I happen to be a representative of that solution," well, now that's an ideal transaction and everybody wins. And then scale that up across an entire economy and you can see why I was saying that sales is the grease that makes the economy work like that and also importantly, brings new technology to the market in a way that makes everything better.
turns.zh: 传统的销售方式就像是，“我要把产品卖给一个‘容易上钩’的人”，或者用一个更极端的例子，“那个人是个超级销售高手，他能把冰块卖给爱斯基摩人”。但说真的，如果你真要把冰块卖给爱斯基摩人，那你就是个混蛋。爱斯基摩人根本不需要冰块啊，除非他们去南加州旅游过。所以，作为销售人员，我更愿意这样向客户解释：你是一位对特定解决方案有特殊偏好的顾问，而你的解决方案正是Atrium。Atrium的最低理想客户量（ICP）可能需要包括销售开发代表（SDR）和客户成功经理（AE）在内的团队，规模在10到300人之间。假如有人说：“我必须成为顶级销售高手，我要买你的软件，皮特。”我会说：“酷。你有多少销售人员？”他们回答：“只有一个。”我会说：“兄弟，我不会卖Atrium给你的。你只会不开心，这很蠢，还会浪费我们的客户成功资源，最后导致客户流失。”（00:34:56）但如果你的做法是：“嘿，我要去市场上寻找那些对我们的技术能解决的问题有高度需求的人，然后和他们探讨他们目前如何解决这个问题。通过一系列提问，我会让他们意识到他们的解决方案可能存在严重问题。一旦通过这种定向提问——也就是所谓的发现阶段——让他们认识到这个问题非常严重，既耗费大量资金，又让他们痛苦不堪，接着我再向他们透露有更好的解决方案，而我恰好就是这个解决方案的代表。”这样一来，交易就达成了双赢。然后将这种模式推广到整个经济体系中，你就能明白为什么我说销售是让经济运转的润滑剂，同时也很重要的是，它能以一种让一切变得更好的方式将新技术推向市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone's listening to this and they're like, "I want to get better at sales, what's one thing I could do differently tomorrow, this week, to improve my ability to sell my product?" What would that be?
turns.zh: 如果有人听了这段内容，问：“我想提高销售能力，从明天或本周起，我能做些什么不同的事来提升销售产品能力？”那会是什么？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: There's the non-complicated version and there's the complicated version. The non-complicated version would just be just walking down the street, make eye contact with everybody, and then every person that you stop next to at Starbucks or the crosswalk or whatever, just strike up a conversation with them, figure out a mechanism by which you can start a conversation with them. Compliment their shirt or their shoes or remark on something. Don't use the weather, because that's lazy, but figure that out, so that's the first version. Probably the more sophisticated version is just be very, very tight on your ICP, just be very, very, very crisp around who has your problem and why. Being more crisp around that and then having that understood is a great way of making sure that you're not wasting time on people who don't have your problem and that you're doing more of those loops with people who are right in the white-hot center. So, one is a behavioral thing and one is a more thoughtful thing.
turns.zh: 有简单版和复杂版之分。简单版就是走在街上，和每个人眼神接触，然后在星巴克、人行横道等地方拦下任何人，和他们聊天，想办法开启对话。比如夸夸他们的衬衫或鞋子，别用天气话题，因为那太老套了，但总归要找到切入点。复杂版就是严格控制理想客户量（ICP），精准锁定有你解决的问题的人群，并清晰传达这一点。更精准地定位目标客户，再让他们理解这一点，这样能确保你不会把时间浪费在没有问题的人身上，而能与真正有需求的人反复沟通。这就是两种不同的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's great. Can you actually explain ICP briefly, because a lot of people may not know that term?
turns.zh: 太好了。你能否简要解释一下ICP（理想客户画像）呢？毕竟很多人可能不了解这个术语。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Thank you. So, ICP stands for Ideal Customer Profile. Actually, it's important to think about there's two things in a B2B sales motion, there's the characteristics of the account, which is the company that's going to buy, and then there's the characteristics of the human and the personas that you're going to be interacting with. Let's use Amplitude as an example. Amplitude's ICP would probably be organizations that make software products, that probably have at least a couple of product managers, because if there's a single product manager, it might be too much, they might be at the point where they don't need a full-blown enterprise analytics suite, and that's probably it. And then on the human side, who are the people who participate in that conversation? Well, the product managers are going to be the ones who are going to be the users, but engineering is probably involved in order to make sure that Amplitude can talk to the cloud data warehouse and so on and so forth, and then moreover, the person who owns the budget might be the VP of product, not the product manager, or it might be the VP of engineering or the CTO. (00:38:18): So, those three different folks that we talked about there, it's different humans. Ideal customer profile is understanding what those parameters look like for looking at an organization in order to say, "Man, that's an awesome op, let's go get in front of them," versus, "Eh, I don't know if that's a very good opportunity, maybe let's pass on that," and then the personas are, "Great, that's an awesome op right there. I know that I'm going to have my first conversation with Lenny, but with an intention that I'm eventually going to get to the VP of product at Airbnb, and that's Suzy over here. And then once we get validation from her, then I know that the VPE over here is Frank," and knowing who the personas are. So, that's what ICP and personas are.
turns.zh: 谢谢。ICP全称是Ideal Customer Profile（理想客户画像）。实际上，在B2B销售流程中，需要考虑两个方面：一是客户公司的特征，二是与你互动的人员的特征。以Amplitude为例，Amplitude的ICP可能包括开发软件产品的公司，这些公司至少应有几位产品经理，因为如果只有一位产品经理，可能说明他们不需要完整的企业级分析套件。另一方面，参与谈判的人员包括产品经理、工程师（确保Amplitude能与云数据仓库等系统集成），以及预算决策者（可能是产品副总裁、工程副总裁或首席技术官）。（00:38:18）我们提到的这三类人员，分别代表不同类型的客户。ICP就是要理解这些参数，判断某个公司是否值得跟进，进而做出决策——比如，“哇，真是个绝佳的机会，让我们去拜访他们吧！”或者“嗯，可能这不是个好机会，还是算了吧！”而人物角色部分则需要明确，比如“太棒了，这次拜访很关键。我知道首先要和Lenny交流，但最终目标是Airbnb的产品副总裁Suzy。一旦得到她的认可，再去找Frank。”所以，ICP和人物角色就是这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. There's a template that you've created that helps you lay out your ICP, so we'll try to link to it in the show notes. I have to find it again.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你制作了一个模板来帮助制定ICP，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。我得再找找看。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Nice. Sounds good.
turns.zh: 不错。听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, we've talked about founder-led sales and how founders should be starting sales, we've talked about just how to get better at sales as a founder, as anyone. I want to talk now about hiring salespeople.
turns.zh: 我们已经讨论了创始人主导的销售，以及创始人应该如何开展销售工作。现在我想谈谈招聘销售人员的问题。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great mug, by the way, Coffee is for Closers. I love it. Can people buy that online or is that just a one-off?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这个杯子很棒，“Coffee is for Closers”（咖啡是为成交高手准备的）。太喜欢了。人们能在网上买到吗？还是只是限量版？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: This is a Modern Sales Pros mugs. I think we have a bunch of Yetis that we give away for Atrium, as well, but we're big onto sales jokes here because you have to... We stole this from New Relic, being very user-centric in your swag, so I've got my Sales Nerds jacket on here, I've got my Let's Get It hat here, I've got my Coffee is for Closers mug. These are all inside sales jokes that maybe your audience won't necessarily get, or maybe they will, but our audience very much gets them. They're like, "Oh man, your hat's so funny. Can you send me one?" I'm like, "No problem. You should buy our software."
turns.zh: 这是Modern Sales Pros的专属杯子。我记得我们也为Atrium送过很多Yeti杯子，但我们特别喜欢用销售相关的梗来活跃气氛。比如我们从New Relic借鉴的用户至上理念，所以我今天穿了Sales Nerds夹克，戴了Let's Get It帽子，用了Coffee is for Closers杯子。这些都是内部的销售笑话，可能听众听不懂，但我们的听众绝对懂。他们会说：“哇，你的帽子太有趣了。能给我一个吗？”我会说：“没问题。但你应该买我们的软件。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it. So, hiring salespeople, we've talked a bit about a lot of these things, like maybe when it's time to hire a salesperson when you're closing a fourth or fifth of your opportunities when this while loop is kicking in. So, in terms of the who to find for this first sales role, and you mentioned that VP of sales are often let go, it's a very high rate of not working out, is that true?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那么，招聘销售人员方面，我们已经讨论过很多相关内容，比如何时该招聘销售人员，比如当你能完成四分之一或五分之一的销售机会时，就说明到了该招聘销售人员的时候了。那么，关于首位销售角色的招聘对象，你提到VP销售职位经常被裁掉，成功率很低，是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Yeah. Again, this is mapped out in the Founder-led Selling presentation and then also in Founding Sales, the book. Generally, what you want to do is you probably don't want to start with a VP of sales to start, a sales leader, and there's a couple of reasons why there. Even if you figured it out yourself, that's required, you have to get to that minimum sufficiency of 10, 20, 30 customers yourself first. But then the reason why I advocate for folks to hire a couple of sellers or a couple of AEs to start is because, again, you have that software in your brain. Unfortunately, there is no GitHub for sales motions, and so it's in your brain, it's in your documents, et cetera, and so now, you're going to teach these other folks. So, what you want to do is you want to hire a couple early-stage pioneer sellers to take that sales motion. (00:41:30): The downside of seeking to hire a VP of sales or a head of sales, or what have you, who actually is a head of sales is coming out of an organization where maybe he or she is a manager of managers or manages eight reps or something like that, is that person hasn't been selling for a hot second. I think actually Jason Lemkin had a pretty funny tweet about this the other day where he was like, "Hiring the VP of sales who's been there and done that before, why exactly does she want to do it again?" Like, "Oh, you scaled up a Datadog or Figma or whatever, you should come to my crappy little startup," it's like, "I'm professionally rich." So, instead, the great folks to look at are the deputies or those early-stage sellers. (00:42:18): So, the example I always use here, my last software company was in recruiting, so if you have a new recruiting technology, my buddy, Troy, runs this recruiting software company called Guide. They make this really cool, guided, hey, hiring process for candidates, whatever, but they sell to recruiting organizations. So the early-stage sellers that he would be interested in would probably be early people at Lever or Greenhouse who sell to the same persona, probably around the same average selling price, but ideally, not an AE who joined Greenhouse last year or two years ago. (00:42:59): Greenhouse just has a phenomenal sales organization, their sales leadership is absolutely fantastic, the gentleman who's the CRO over there is a good friend of mine, Sean Murray. But early-stage selling takes early-stage sellers or people who have been there, because you're not going to have all the collateral, slides and scripts and whatever aren't going to be all buttoned up and with a bow around them, and so looking for those early-stage, grimier, grittier sellers is a more effective way of going about that. Those are the folks that you want to look for once you've gotten to that statistical significance of your own selling capacity.
turns.zh: 是的。再次说明，这在《创始人主导的销售》演示文稿和《创始人销售》一书中都有详细阐述。通常，你可能不希望一开始就招聘VP销售或销售主管，主要有几个原因。即使你自己能搞定这些事务，但你必须先自己摸索出最基本的客户开发流程，比如如何获取10、20、30个客户。但我之所以建议先招聘几个销售先锋，是因为你已经掌握了销售流程。不幸的是，销售流程没有GitHub这样的平台来存储，所以这些流程都存在于你的脑海中、文档里等等，现在你需要把这些知识传授给其他人。所以，你需要招聘几个早期阶段的销售先锋，让他们来执行这些销售流程。（00:41:30）：招聘有过VP销售或销售主管经验的人的缺点在于，他们可能来自一个组织，在那里他们是管理者中的管理者，或者管理着8个销售代表之类的，但他们已经很久没有实际销售过了。我记得Jason Lemkin前几天发了一条很有趣的推文，他说：“招聘那些‘经验丰富’的VP销售，他们为什么还要再来一次呢？”比如，“你成功管理过Datadog或Figma之类的公司，那你为什么还要来我这家小创业公司呢？”这就像是在说“我已经财务自由了”。所以，更好的选择是副手或早期阶段的销售人员。（00:42:18）：我常举的例子是，我上一家软件公司是做招聘的，如果你有新的招聘技术，我的朋友Troy经营一家叫Guide的招聘软件公司。他们为候选人开发了一个非常酷的、指导性的招聘流程等等。但他们面向的是招聘机构。所以他感兴趣的早期销售人员很可能是Lever或Greenhouse的早期员工，他们面向的是相同的客户群体，平均销售价格也相似，但理想情况下，最好不是1-2年前加入Greenhouse的AE。（00:42:59）：Greenhouse的销售团队非常出色，他们的销售领导团队也非常棒，那里的CRO肖恩·默里是我很好的朋友。但早期阶段的销售需要早期阶段的销售人员或有过相关经验的人，因为你不会拥有所有完备的资料、演示文稿和脚本之类的东西，这些东西不会包装得漂漂亮亮、井井有条。因此，寻找那些早期阶段、更接地气、更坚韧的销售人员，是更有效的途径。一旦你自己的销售能力达到了统计学意义上的显著水平，这才是你应该寻找的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make that just even clearer, the suggestion is if you're, say, a Series A founder, what's a profile of a person you look for? You said it's a deputy at a successful sales org?
turns.zh: 再说得更清楚一点，建议是，如果你是一位A轮融资的创始人，理想的招聘对象是什么样的？你说应该找成功销售组织中的副手？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I'll give you a couple examples. I don't know, say you're doing some sort of design tool, I would go look at the Figma sales organization and I would look at some of the earlier sellers who were there maybe two years ago or three years ago or what have you, maybe you could consider getting a sales manager there who's not super far from selling. A great example of this is there's this woman, Marissa Fuhrer, who works at Figma, she's absolutely fantastic. She works on the enterprise team there and she was at Dropbox previously as a seller for a long time. (00:44:24): She would be a great profile for someone who's not too far from having sold and is willing to roll up her sleeves, but ideally, that would probably be the person who you'd want to hire after you've hired those couple of sellers and gotten them to success. Because the other thing, too, with Marissa, she's probably going to look at your organization and be like, "Cool. Prove to me that your product fits the market, because I don't want to necessarily take a bet on you," and then you would say, "Well, in addition to having a 25% win rate with me, I have these two sellers right here and they both have 20% win rates and you can see that they're both closing $50,000 of bookings a month, all I need you to do is scale it up." In which case, that early stage head of sales is like, "Let's do it."
turns.zh: 我举几个例子。比如说，你正在开发某种设计工具，我会去研究Figma的销售团队，观察那些两三年前就在那里工作的早期销售人员，或许你可以考虑从他们中挖来一位销售经理。马丽莎·福勒（Marissa Fuhrer）就是个绝佳的例子，她在Figma的企业团队工作，此前曾在Dropbox担任长期销售人员。（00:44:24）她会是那种离真正销售不远、愿意亲力亲为的人选。但理想情况下，这类人才应该是在你成功招募了几个销售人员、并帮助他们取得业绩后，再考虑引入的。因为马丽莎也会审视你的团队，可能会说：“不错，但你得先证明你的产品符合市场需求，我可不想冒险。”你可以回应：“除了我25%的成单率外，我还有两个销售人员，他们的成单率都是20%，而且每月都能完成5万美元的订单量。现在只需要你把这个规模扩大就行。”这样一来，初期销售负责人就会说：“那就开始吧。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: She's about to get a bunch of LinkedIn requests.
turns.zh: 她马上就会收到一堆领英请求。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: She's great. This is one of the things that we really love at Atrium, is we have really great customers. We're creating a new category of software and so it's one of those things where more advanced, more modern sales managers and leaders really get it, that's how it always is in category creation. But when you find the people who really get it and really get it, they turn out to be awesome. That's one of the things that just makes startups fantastic.
turns.zh: 她太棒了。在Atrium，我们最引以为傲的就是拥有优质的客户群体。我们正在开创一个新类别的软件，通常在这种创新领域，经验丰富的现代销售管理者和领导者能深切理解其中的奥秘。这正是品类创新中常有的现象。但当你找到真正领悟其精髓的人时，他们往往会大放异彩。这正是初创公司魅力所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a sign that maybe it's not working out when you hire your either first salesperson or maybe first five, what are signs? Because you said it often does not work out, what are early signals like, "We should rethink this"?
turns.zh: 当你招聘首位销售人员或前五位销售人员时，如何判断是否行不通？因为你提到成功率往往不高，有哪些早期信号能预示需要重新评估？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: This is another reason why it's really important to do it yourself to start, but presuming that you've been able to close business on a reliable basis, again, with arm's length prospects, it can't be Lenny's mother-in-law buying my software-
turns.zh: 这也是为什么亲自操刀至关重要的另一个原因。但假设你已经能与真实客户达成可靠的交易——当然，不能是莱尼的岳母购买我的软件——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Huge fan, for real, actually, she is.
turns.zh: 说真的，我真是她的超级粉丝。

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: God bless, but she's not ICP for Atrium. This is the danger of doing revenue trades in your accelerator or whatever, it's not real. So, if you have done that and you've sold 20 or 30 deals, you know it can be done, we have an existence proof of this. So, if someone else can't do it the way that you do it, and this is why hiring two folks to start is effective, you don't want to hire just one, maybe three, but four, it's like, "Ugh, that's a lot to manage," at least to start. So, if you have done that and the person, their win rates are poor or their activity levels are poor, things like that, those are usually indicators that it's not work out, that they're not getting those second dates, they're not getting those third dates, but importantly, they have to have the materials in question. (00:47:11): Did you create the slide deck? Did you take people through and did you give it to them? Did you take all the discovery questions that were in your brain and write them down into a Google Doc or a Notion page or what have you? Do you have a demo script for them? If those things are not present, then probably no one's going to be successful, or at least they're going to have to rederive all that stuff that you already did. But if you have all those precursors and it's not sticking for someone, that's probably a good leading indicator that they're not going to work out
turns.zh: 愿上帝保佑，但她不是Atrium的ICP。这就是在加速器或其他平台做收益交易的危险之处——那不是真实的。所以，如果你曾这么做过，并且成功完成了20到30笔交易，那说明这确实可行，我们已经有了这个成功案例。但如果别人无法按照你的方式去做，这就是为什么招聘两人入职比单人更有效的原因——你不应该只招一个，而是三个甚至四个。至少在初期阶段，这会让人觉得“哎呀，管理起来太麻烦了”。如果你发现新人胜率低、活动量不足之类的问题，这些通常都是不成功的迹象——他们拿不到第二次约见机会，更别提第三次了。但最重要的是，他们必须掌握相关材料。（00:47:11）：你制作了幻灯片吗？你有没有带新人过一遍并把材料交给他们？你有没有把脑海中的探索性问题整理成Google Doc或Notion页面之类的？你有没有为他们准备演示脚本？如果这些条件都不具备，那大概没人能成功，或者至少他们得重新整理你已经做好的所有材料。但如果你准备了这些基础材料，新人还是不行，那很可能就是他们不适合这个岗位的预警信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much time do you give these folks before you make a decision?
turns.zh: 在做决定之前，你会给这些人多长时间的观察期？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: This is why it's so, so, so important to look at leading indicators. This is something that we just think about all the time here at Atrium, from a instrumentation and data-driven sales management, is if someone's not having customer-facing meetings, if they're low activity, you're never going to win anything. If you have a 50% win rate on two opportunities in a month, that's probably still not going to be super helpful unless you have a very, very, very high deal size. So, looking at those leading indicators like, "Are they having first meetings? Are they having second meetings? What does their email volume look like? Are they progressing things through, are they getting things to proposal, and then eventually, are things closing?" (00:48:24): I do a bunch of masterclasses for Atrium on data-driven sales management and one of them is on ramping. It's called Ramping For Success, I forget the name of the masterclass, but looking at those leading indicators like opportunity inflow, "Is a person putting meetings on their calendar, are they progressing them? Are they being active in the meantime?" Those are all really good leading indicators. If somebody's not getting first meetings on the calendar, you know within a month, it's like, "Cool, this isn't working out." (00:48:54): Now, if they're not getting to second or third meetings, but they are getting those first meetings, well, now you know you've got a different problem, which they're getting those first dates, but they're not getting a second date and they're not getting a second date the same way that you were, maybe that's a coaching issue or maybe it's just a behavioral problem that's that you're not going to be able to surmount. But the point is having instrumentation on the most leading indicator possible gives you eyes onto whether or not things are working or not and you can make judgements fast, because the worst possible situation is nine months in, you're like, "Man, it's not working." It's like, "Man, I bet if you looked at the leading indicators, you would have known two months in this wasn't working."
turns.zh: 这就是为什么关注领先指标如此、如此、如此重要。在Atrium，我们一直从仪表盘和数据驱动的销售管理角度思考这个问题：如果某人不参加面向客户的会议，如果他们的活动量很低，你就永远无法达成交易。即使你一个月内有两个机会达成了50%的成功率，如果交易规模不大，这可能也意义不大。因此，关注这些领先指标至关重要，比如他们是否参加了首次会议？是否参加了第二次会议？他们的邮件量如何？他们是否在推进项目？是否能将项目推进到提案阶段，最终是否能成功签单？（00:48:24）：我为Atrium做了很多关于数据驱动销售管理的大师课，其中一个是关于新人入职的，叫做《成功入职指南》，我忘了这个大师课的具体名称了。但关注那些领先指标，比如机会流入量，"某人是否把会议安排进了日历，是否在推进项目？"这些都是非常好的领先指标。如果某人一个月内连首次会议都安排不了，那你就知道这行不通了。（00:48:54）：现在，如果他们没能进入第二次或第三次会议，但第一次会议安排得不错，那你就知道存在其他问题——他们能安排第一次会议，但无法推进到第二次。这可能是指导问题，也可能是行为问题，但这些问题你可能无法克服。但关键是尽可能多地关注领先指标，这样你就能及时判断事情是否进展顺利，并迅速做出判断。最糟糕的情况是，九个月后你才意识到"天哪，这根本行不通"。其实早在两个月前，你通过关注领先指标就能发现问题了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you gave us a bottom end of the range like, "In a month, you should be able to know, a lot of times." What would be the max by which like, "If things are going okay, by six months, it's probably going to be good," or what is that timeframe?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你给我们一个下限，比如"一个月内，你应该能知道，很多时候"。那么上限是什么呢？"如果一切顺利，六个月后应该会不错"，或者这个时间范围是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Oh, where you know you're successful?
turns.zh: 哦，就是你知道这个人能成功的时候？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It sounds like maybe from a month to some future month, this is a period where you can get a sense of this person is going to work out. What's that range, in your mind?
turns.zh: 是的。听起来可能从一个月到未来某个月，这是一个你能判断这个人是否能成功的时期。在你看来，时间范围是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: It's almost like you're continuously monitoring. In the first month, maybe you spend that time onboarding the rep, teaching them, going through mock discovery conversations, mock demos, et cetera, having them ride along with you. In the second month, we would expect them to have 10 first meetings or maybe 20 first meetings and we would expect 50% of those to get to the second meetings, and we would measure those things. In the third month, we would expect some subset of those first meetings and second meetings that happened in the second month to get to a proposal, to get to a commercial conversation, and then maybe we would expect some of the deals in that month to close to win, or maybe the next month. (00:50:38): It's essentially like you're looking at the leading indicators in the appropriate timeframe, such that if someone is in month three and they're getting a bunch of their deals to proposal, you can't declare victory yet because the money is not in the bank, however things are looking good. So, if you get to month four and lots of things are getting to proposal, but nothing's closing in month four and nothing's closing in month five, you still can't say "Olly olly oxen free," you should still be very concerned. But if the leading indicator is at the right level for the right period or right interval in ramp, then you can feel confident, but not declare victory yet.
turns.zh:
这几乎就像你一直在持续监控情况。在第一个月，也许你会把时间花在新销售人员的入职培训上，教他们如何开展业务，模拟探索性对话、演示等，并陪同他们一起上门拜访。在第二个月，我们预计他们会完成10次或20次首次拜访，其中50%的客户能推进到第二次对话阶段，我们会对这些数据进行跟踪。在第三个月，我们希望第二个月完成的首次和第二次对话中，有一部分能推进到提案阶段，进而展开商业洽谈。最终，可能有一些交易会在当月或下月达成。

（00:50:38）本质上，就是在适当的时间段内关注领先指标。例如，如果某位销售人员进入第三个月，却只有少数交易进入提案阶段，你就不能因此宣告成功，因为钱还没到账，尽管情况看似乐观。但如果到了第四个月，大量交易进入提案阶段，却没有任何交易在第四或第五个月完成，你就仍不能掉以轻心。但如果领先指标在正确的时间段或周期内达到了合理水平，你就可以感到放心，但暂时还不能宣告成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Something that this is reminding me of is we are chatting ahead of this call and you mentioned that working from home is really bad for salespeople, in your experience. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 明白了。这让我想起之前的交流，你提到在家办公对销售人员不利，根据你的经验，能否谈谈这一点？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: It's primarily bad for junior salespeople. Senior salespeople have been selling out in what's known as the field for a long time, but when you think about the behavior that we're talking about, which is learning, so what needs to happen? The new sellers, they need to learn the sales motion and then they need to be audited, instrumented, so the faster the loops are on that, the better off you're going to be. If the loops are once a day of listening to their calls or maybe even a longer interval, then just the correction loops are just going to be way too slow, versus if you're sitting next to somebody or you're sitting amongst three or four people and listening to all their calls concurrently and then they get off of a call and it's like, "Hey, that was really good, correction here, correction here, correction here, correction here. Here, run it back to me." (00:52:28): Now, the loops, the speed with which you're able to update their software and make sure that the sales motion is running appropriately on them, is quite high. In early-stage startups, that's the only thing that matters, it's a race against time to make sure that you get to success, so you can raise your next round of financing or get to profitability or what have you, and so having asynchronous distance is really problematic for that, especially for junior folks, like SDRs, junior AEs, all of that, it really is problematic. Once that sales motion is baked and can be distributed, that's potentially a different situation, but very early on, having someone being able to sit side-by-side with your sellers, t's hard to beat.
turns.zh: 这对初级销售人员影响最为不利。资深销售人员长期在外地开展业务，但就我们所讨论的学习行为而言，关键在于：新销售人员需要掌握销售流程，随后接受审计和反馈。审计和反馈的频率越高，效果越显著。如果每天只听一次通话录音，或者间隔更久，那么纠错周期就会过慢。而如果销售人员身处办公室，或与三四人共处一室，实时听取所有通话录音，结束后立即给予反馈：“嘿，刚才表现不错，这里需要调整，这里需要调整，这里需要调整。再来一遍让我听听。” （00:52:28）现在，审计和反馈的速度至关重要。在初创公司阶段，速度是唯一重要因素——你必须与时间赛跑，确保成功达成融资、实现盈利等目标。因此，异地办公对初级员工（如销售开发代表、初级客户成功经理等）影响极大。一旦销售流程成熟并可规模化应用，情况或许会有所不同，但在早期阶段，让销售人员身处办公室办公确实是最优选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what's the solution, if you're starting, now, a B2B company, your advice is, "Don't be remote, work in an office"?
turns.zh: 那么，如果你现在要创办一家B2B公司，建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: My point of view on that is, especially at early stage, from a founder's standpoint, being shoulder-to-shoulder with your co-founders certainly, but even a founder who has a couple of sellers that they're working with, being side-by-side with them in order to help them learn faster, teach them more, have accountability, and then have training loops is really what you need to do. Because the alternative is there's a whole generation of SDRs who are, it's kind of like learning loss, if you will, there's a bunch of 24 year olds who have never learned the skills that are needed at the same way, at the same clip, that they would have sitting amongst 10 others with an SDR manager sitting in the middle of them, or an AE manager sitting in the middle of them.
turns.zh: 关于这一点，我的观点是，尤其是在早期阶段，从创始人的角度来看，与联合创始人并肩作战固然重要，但即便是一位有几位销售人员合作的创始人，也需要与他们并肩同行，以帮助他们更快地学习、传授更多知识、确保责任落实，并开展培训循环。这才是你真正需要做的。因为另一种情况是，会有一整代销售开发代表（SDR）出现某种程度上的学习缺失。比如，许多24岁的年轻人从未以同样的方式、同样的速度掌握所需技能，而如果他们与其他10位同事共处一室，并有销售开发经理或客户成功经理在中间协调指导，情况就会大不相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any last pieces of wisdom before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么最后的智慧之言吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I think probably the biggest thing is, the thing that I just like to encourage founders and product managers and what have you, is just don't be afraid of sales. There's a lot of people out there who would love to tell you a story that it's magical or like, "Oh, you've got to be a born seller," or things like that and it's really not. Those people are just talking their book, if you will, and so just getting good at those behaviors, it's going to benefit you in a myriad of ways. Even if you don't want to necessarily be an early-stage founder, even as a product manager within an enterprise organization or even a consumer organization, selling behaviors and good communication and persuasion and always thinking about what's in it for them, et cetera, those are really good skills for internal selling, for external selling, if you want to interface with customers, et cetera. All these skills are very important and impactful for a myriad of personas.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的一点是，我想鼓励创始人、产品经理等人士，不要对销售望而却步。外面有很多人，他们会告诉你销售是神奇的，或者“哦，你必须天生就是销售人才”之类的话，但事实并非如此。这些人不过是在夸大其词罢了。所以，掌握这些销售技能会让你受益匪浅。即使你不想成为初创企业的创始人，即使是在企业或消费者组织中担任产品经理，具备销售能力、良好的沟通和说服能力，以及始终为客户着想等品质，都对内部销售和外部销售大有裨益。如果你需要与客户沟通，所有这些技能都非常重要，对不同角色都具有深远影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, with that, we've reached the very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you, we're going to go through it pretty fast. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你，我们会很快结束。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I am.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Question one, what are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，您最推荐给其他人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: The books that I recommend the most, there would be The Goal by Eli Goldratt. There are two books that inspired Atrium, one is the Goal, which is essentially is a novelization of the Toyota lean manufacturing system, so it's a process engineering book written as a novel, it's really fantastic. Sales organizations are just revenue factories, so if you want to think about systems thinking and processes, but in a way that's not a textbook, it's absolutely fantastic. (00:56:01): And then the other one is a book by Bill Walsh called The Score Takes Care of itself. Bill Walsh is a really famous football coach for the Stanford Cardinals and the San Francisco 49ers and he just broke down how you can't worry about the score in the football game, you can only worry about the things that are in front of you, that you can control, and that if you do a high quantity of high-quality actions, whatever your position is, as a quarterback or a linebacker running back or whatever, then the score will take care of itself. That's very applicable to sales, as well, if you focus on those leading indicators and make sure that you're doing it in a high quantity of high quality way, then the score will take care of itself. So, those are two great books I like to recommend to folks.
turns.zh: 我最推荐的书籍当中，《目标》（The Goal）是埃利·戈德拉特（Eli Goldratt）所著。这本书对Atrium产生了深远影响，其中一本灵感来源是《目标》。这本书本质上是丰田精益生产系统的通俗化解析，可以说是一本以小说形式呈现的流程工程学著作，实在令人惊叹。销售组织不过是营收工厂，所以如果你想从非教科书的角度思考系统思维与流程设计，这本书绝对值得一读。（00:56:01）另一本是比尔·沃尔什（Bill Walsh）的《比分会照顾自己》（The Score Takes Care of Itself）。比尔·沃尔什是斯坦福红雀队和旧金山49人队的著名橄榄球教练，他剖析了在橄榄球比赛中不必过度关注比分的道理——你只需专注于眼前可控的任务。只要高频、高质地完成每项动作，无论你身处何种位置——四分卫、线卫、跑卫等——比分自然会水到渠成。这本书对销售同样适用，只要专注于领先指标，确保高质量地完成大量任务，比分自然会呈现。以下是我最想推荐的两本好书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite other podcasts?
turns.zh: 你还喜欢其他播客吗？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Oh boy, I don't listen to too many. I listen to Lenny's and I listen to the All-In Podcast, just so I can get my fill of doom and gloom.
turns.zh: 天哪，我听得不多。我听莱尼（Lenny）的播客，也听《全力以赴》（All-In Podcast），这样才能满足我对悲观情绪的需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And knowledge, with this one. Favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 还有知识类的。最近你有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I've got a five-year-old, so we're all Disney all the time, so I think probably the one that's been on repeat recently has been Encanto. There you go.
turns.zh: 我有个五岁的孩子，所以我们一直在看迪士尼动画片，最近反复看的是《魔法满屋》（Encanto）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that one. Favorite interview question that you like to ask folks?
turns.zh: 我超爱那部片子。你最喜欢提问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: So, I'm going to change this up on you, it's less about interview questions. One of the things I'm a really big fan of is job simulation, especially in sales, and so I'm a big fan of doing screens, so we actually have a written screen that we do with folks, where it's the Google Doc that has a dozen or so biographical questions that we allow people to answer. You'd be shocked at how well it screens people, 57% people won't do it. These are not complicated questions, it's like, "Lenny, tell me about something that you've built that you're proud of," it's a dozen of those questions. So, one, you can filter out people who are not serious, you can filter out people who have low levels of give a shit. You also can see whether or not people can communicate in a compelling fashion with a beginning, a middle, and an end. You can also see their attention to detail, whether or not it's ridden with typos or they forget to answer some of them or what have you. So, it's not an interview question thing, but that's a huge hiring hack, from my perspective.
turns.zh: 那我换个话题吧，这跟面试问题关系不大。工作模拟，尤其是销售领域，我特别推崇。实际上，我们有一套筛选工具——谷歌文档里有十几个个人经历类问题，面试者可以自由回答。令人惊讶的是，57%的人都不愿意完成这个筛选。这些问题并不复杂，比如“莱尼，讲讲你引以为傲的作品”，十来个这类问题。通过这个筛选，你能淘汰掉不认真的候选人，筛选出缺乏敬业精神的人，还能观察他们是否能用开头、过程、结尾的结构进行有效沟通，观察他们的细节意识，比如是否有拼写错误、是否遗漏回答等。所以这不是面试问题，而是从我的角度看来，一个非常有效的招聘技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a form that folks fill out when they're trying to apply to work at Atrium, is that right?
turns.zh: 这就是人们申请Atrium时填写的表格，对吧？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: Yeah. Or it's just something that for all my portfolio companies, as well, that people just use it. It's a Google Doc and you just clone it, give it to them, "You have edit rights, let me know when it's done." You'd be shocked, people are like, "Oh, I didn't forgot to do it." Great, you told me everything I need.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过对我所有的投资组合公司来说，人们都会用这个方法。就是用谷歌文档，克隆一份文件后发给对方，告诉他们：“你有编辑权限，完成后记得通知我。”你肯定会惊讶地发现，人们会说：“哦，我差点忘了做这件事。”太棒了，你已经把我需要的都讲清楚了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Final question, do you have a favorite story of you or a salesperson closing an awesome deal, something that seemed impossible, something that you're proud of?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题，你有没有什么喜欢的故事，讲讲你或销售团队成功拿下某个大单的故事，哪怕看似不可能完成的任务，只要能让人倍感自豪就行？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: There's a gentleman in our sales organization named Sean, who was an early seller here, he's now a sales manager, he is absolutely fantastic. I think one of the things that early-stage founders and also sellers have to remember is you're, generally speaking, not going to close the deal on the first time through the pipe. As we discussed earlier, if you have a 30% win rate, that's pretty great. If you have a 20% win rate, that's pretty solid, but that still means that four out of five are not going to close, but the next time around, they might, so win rate on the second time through the pipeline. (00:59:21): So, Sean closed, one of our biggest customers is a company called GRIN, they're absolutely fantastic. They make influencer management software for brands, very cool stuff. I think Sean probably ran three or four ops with them before we were able to get a toehold in the account a couple years ago, they were much smaller, and so now, I think they have 100 SDRs and 80 AEs that are being managed using Atrium. So, I think there's a good lesson there, which is it's not necessarily going to be the first time through the pipe and it's maybe not the second time, but you just have to keep pushing that boulder up the hill and eventually, when you do, good things happen.
turns.zh: 我们销售团队有个叫肖恩的成员，他是早期销售人员，现在已经是销售经理了，他真的非常出色。我觉得初创公司创始人和销售人员需要记住的一点是，通常第一次过销售流程是很难成功的。正如我们之前讨论的，如果胜率达到30%已经很不错了，20%也很稳妥，但这意味着五次中有四次都无法达成交易。不过下一次再试试看，胜率或许就会提高。（00:59:21）肖恩成功拿下了我们最大的客户之一——GRIN公司。他们为品牌提供网红管理软件，非常棒。我记得几年前GRIN还很小的时候，肖恩和他们合作了三四次才成功进入客户名单。现在他们有100名销售开发代表和80名客户成功经理，都在使用Atrium平台进行管理。这充分说明了耐心坚持的重要性，最终一定会有好结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a great lesson to leave us with, very empowering. Pete, this was everything I hoped it would be. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, more about Atrium, the book, and then how can folks be useful to you?
turns.zh: 真是个振聋发聩的启示，太鼓舞人心了。皮特，这次访谈完全符合我的期待。最后两个问题：如果读者想了解更多关于Atrium的信息，包括书籍内容，或者想为你提供帮助，该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Pete Kazanjy
turns.en: I'm pretty easy to find online, I'm the only Pete Kazanjy in the United States, as far as I can tell. Google will autocorrect my name if you Google it wrong, so that's pretty helpful. Find me on LinkedIn, find me on Twitter. You can also find Founding Sales at foundingsales.com, as Lenny notes. The whole book is available online as hypertext, you can buy a physical copy, as well, but the reason why my wife put it into a Squarespace site was because we wanted people to be able to search it and come back to it and use it as a reference and so on and so forth.
